name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle (descent stage)
modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Apollo Lunar Module (only the descent stage is shown)

pairedModels.label: EASEP
pairedModels.modelCredit: Simplified model built for this game (no NASA 3D model exists for it)

story.whatItIs: Eagle was the two-stage lunar module that carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to the Moon's surface. Its descent stage, which you found, is what remains at the landing site.
story.whyLeft: The descent stage was the launch platform for the ascent stage, so it stayed on the Moon when the ascent stage lifted off on 21 July 1969. The ascent stage docked with the Command/Service Module and was then jettisoned into lunar orbit on 22 July.
story.science: Eagle carried the Early Apollo Scientific Experiment Package (EASEP), a 48 kg set of self-contained instruments: a passive seismometer, a lunar dust detector and a laser ranging retroreflector, with solar panels for power. It was turned on on 21 July 1969, worked even though temperatures ran 30 °C above the planned maximum, and stopped accepting commands on 27 August 1969.
story.nowStatus: The descent stage is at 0.67416° N, 23.47314° E in Mare Tranquilitatis, a position NASA determined from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images. NASA's catalog page does not describe its present condition.

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 11 Lunar Module / EASEP (1969-059C)

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Module Falcon, ALSEP and rover
modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Apollo Lunar Module (only the descent stage is shown)

pairedModels.label: ALSEP
pairedModels.modelCredit: Simplified model built for this game (no NASA 3D model exists for it)

pairedModels.label: Lunar Roving Vehicle
pairedModels.modelCredit: Simplified model built for this game (no NASA 3D model exists for it)

story.whatItIs: Falcon was Apollo 15's two-stage lunar module. David Scott and James Irwin landed in it at the foot of the Apennine Mountains, and over three moonwalks (18 hours 35 minutes) the crew covered 27.9 km in the Lunar Roving Vehicle and collected 77.31 kg of samples.
story.whyLeft: The descent stage was left on the Moon as the launch platform for the ascent stage. The ascent stage lifted off on 2 August 1971, docked with the Command/Service Module, and was jettisoned on 3 August. The ALSEP stayed to keep recording until 1977.
story.science: The ALSEP had seven instruments: they measured seismic activity, the magnetic field, solar wind, suprathermal ions, the atmosphere, dust and heat flow. A SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generator powered it with about 70 W at launch and 63.5 W after one year.
story.nowStatus: The descent stage is at 26.13239° N, 3.63330° E, and the ALSEP central station nearby (26.1341° N, 3.6298° E) was shut down on 30 September 1977. The ascent stage crashed into the Moon at 26.36° N, 0.25° E.

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 15 Lunar Module / ALSEP (1971-063C)

name: Apollo 12 Lunar Module Intrepid and ALSEP
modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Apollo Lunar Module (only the descent stage is shown)

pairedModels.label: ALSEP
pairedModels.modelCredit: Simplified model built for this game (no NASA 3D model exists for it)

story.whatItIs: Intrepid carried Pete Conrad and Alan Bean to Oceanus Procellarum, the Ocean of Storms. It landed on 19 November 1969, within about 180 m of the Surveyor 3 lander.
story.whyLeft: The descent stage was left on the Moon as the launch platform for the ascent stage, which lifted off on 20 November 1969 and docked with the command module. The ascent stage was then jettisoned and deliberately crashed into the Moon about 60 km from the Apollo 12 seismic station, creating the first recorded artificial moonquake.
story.science: The astronauts set up an ALSEP with a passive seismometer, suprathermal ion detector, cold cathode ion gauge, lunar dust detector, lunar surface magnetometer and solar wind spectrometer, powered by a SNAP-27 generator. The crew also collected about 34.35 kg of rock and soil, a solar wind foil, and about 10 kg of Surveyor 3 parts.
story.nowStatus: The descent stage is at 3.0128° S, 23.4219° W. The ALSEP central station (3.0094° S, 23.4246° W) was shut down, with all ALSEP stations, on 30 September 1977.

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 12 Lunar Module / ALSEP (1969-099C)

name: Surveyor 3
modelCredit: Simplified model built for this game (no NASA 3D model exists for it)

story.whatItIs: A robotic lander launched on 17 April 1967 and landed on 20 April 1967. It sent back 6,326 TV pictures and used a surface sampler, which could reach up to 5 feet and dig 7 inches deep, to dig four trenches, run four bearing tests and perform thirteen impact tests.
story.whyLeft: Its landing was rough: reflective rocks confused the descent radar and the main engine did not cut off at the right altitude, so it bounced twice before settling. Its last contact was on 4 May 1967, two days after the lunar night began, and it stayed where it landed.
story.science: The soil behaved like wet sand with a bearing strength of about 10 psi (98 kPa), so the surface was judged solid enough to support an Apollo Lunar Module. In November 1969 Apollo 12 landed about 180 m away, and astronauts recovered parts, including the soil scoop and camera system, to study the effects of about two and a half years on the Moon.
story.nowStatus: Surveyor 3 is inactive at its landing site in southeastern Oceanus Procellarum (about 3° S, 23.41° W). NASA's page does not describe its present condition.

name: Sojourner rover and Pathfinder lander
modelCredit: Simplified model built for this game (no NASA 3D model exists for it)

pairedModels.label: Pathfinder lander
pairedModels.modelCredit: Simplified model built for this game (no NASA 3D model exists for it)

story.whatItIs: Sojourner was a 10.6 kg (23 lb) rover, the first robotic rover delivered to the Martian surface. It rolled down the ramp of the Pathfinder lander, named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station, late on sol 2 (the night of 5 July 1997).
story.whyLeft: Pathfinder landed at Ares Vallis on 4 July 1997 and the mission ended on 27 September 1997 with its final data transmission. NASA's mission page does not give a reason for the end of operations.
story.science: The instruments included an Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer, three cameras and an atmospheric structure and weather package. Rounded pebbles and cobbles pointed to rock formed in running water, suggesting Mars was once warm and wet. The mission also found magnetic airborne dust, dust devils and early morning water-ice clouds, and returned 2.3 billion bits of data, including over 16,500 lander images and 550 rover images.
story.nowStatus: The mission ended in 1997. NASA's mission page does not give coordinates for the site or describe the condition of the hardware.

sources.title: NASA GISS Mars24: Mars lander coordinates (map position only; Ingenuity uses the Jezero Crater landing site of Perseverance)

name: Spirit rover
modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Mars Exploration Rover (Opportunity, MER-B); used here for its twin, Spirit

story.whatItIs: Spirit was one of NASA's twin Mars Exploration Rovers, with Opportunity. It launched on 10 June 2003 and landed on 3 January 2004 in Gusev Crater, at 14.5692° S, 175.4729° E, about 13.4 km from its planned target. The site was named Columbia Memorial Station.
story.whyLeft: On 1 May 2009 Spirit became stuck in soft soil beside the western edge of a feature called Home Plate, and on 28 November 2009 its right rear wheel stopped working. Contact was lost after 22 March 2010. More than 1,300 commands were sent without success; NASA says the most probable cause was excessive cold that made its survival heaters ineffective. NASA ended recovery efforts and declared the mission complete on 25 May 2011.
story.science: Spirit found varied bedrock in the Columbia Hills, with some rocks altered by water, filmed dust devils in motion, and found evidence of an ancient explosion at Home Plate. In 2007 it unearthed nearly pure silica, which NASA calls strong evidence that ancient Mars was much wetter. It drove 4.8 miles (7.73 km) and worked for 6 years, 2 months and 19 days, more than 25 times its intended lifetime.
story.nowStatus: Spirit is no longer operating. It is in Gusev Crater, where it became stuck beside Home Plate.

sources.title: NASA Science: Mars Exploration Rover Spirit

name: Opportunity rover
modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Mars Exploration Rover (Opportunity, MER-B)

story.whatItIs: Opportunity was one of NASA's twin Mars Exploration Rovers, with Spirit. It launched on 7 July 2003 and landed in January 2004 on Meridiani Planum, at 1.9483° S, 354.47417° E, about 14.9 km from its intended target. It came down inside Eagle crater. (NASA's page gives both 24 and 25 January for the landing.)
story.whyLeft: A severe Mars-wide dust storm blanketed the rover's location in June 2018, cutting the power available to its solar panels. Its last signal was heard on 10 June 2018, and NASA declared the end of the mission on 13 February 2019.
story.science: Opportunity found evidence that Mars may once have been able to sustain microbial life. Near its heat shield it found an iron-nickel meteorite, and it explored Victoria and Endeavour craters and Marathon Valley. It drove 28.06 miles (45.16 km) in total, passing the marathon distance on 25 March 2015, which NASA says made it the first human enterprise to do so on another world.
story.nowStatus: Opportunity is no longer operating. NASA says its final resting spot is Perseverance Valley.

sources.title: NASA Science: Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity

story.whatItIs: Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976 on the western slopes of Chryse Planitia, about 28 km from its planned target. It sent back high-quality color photographs and a 300-degree panorama, and recorded temperatures from about −86 °C before dawn to about −33 °C in the afternoon.
story.whyLeft: The lander stopped operating on 11 November 1982 after a faulty command sent from Earth interrupted communications. Later attempts to regain contact failed. It had operated for just over six years after landing.
story.science: On 28 July 1976 its robot arm collected the first soil samples for its biological lab and gas chromatograph mass spectrometer. The data could have been read as a weak indication of life, but the major organic-compound test was negative, and the soil showed an abundance of sulfur. Its seismometer did not work.
story.nowStatus: The lander is no longer operating, at 22.483° N, 47.94° W. It was renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station in January 1982.

story.whatItIs: Viking 2 was a combined orbiter and lander mission to Mars, launched on 9 September 1975 from Cape Canaveral, Florida. Its lander touched down on 3 September 1976 in Utopia Planitia, about 6,460 km from the Viking 1 landing site, at 47.968° N, 225.71° W.
story.whyLeft: The lander transmitted data until 12 April 1980. NASA's page does not say what ended its transmissions. The Viking 2 orbiter's operations had ended earlier, on 24 July 1978, after a series of leaks.
story.science: Its soil biology experiments, which began on 12 September 1976, gave results similar to Viking 1's: inconclusive on whether life exists or ever existed on Mars. Together the two Viking orbiters returned 52,663 images and mapped about 97% of the surface, and the two landers returned about 4,500 photos of their landing sites.
story.nowStatus: The lander is no longer operating, in Utopia Planitia. In July 2001 it was renamed the Gerald Soffen Memorial Station, after the Viking project scientist.

name: InSight lander
modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, InSight Cruise Lander (arm deployed)

story.whatItIs: InSight launched on 5 May 2018 and landed on 26 November 2018 on the western side of Elysium Planitia. It carried a seismometer and a heat flow probe, which its robotic arm placed on the surface.
story.whyLeft: NASA lists the mission as ended on 15 December 2022. The challenge description says the lander eventually lost power; the mission page does not spell out a cause.
story.science: Marsquake data revealed a "lumpy" interior, with rocky impact material scattered through the mantle. The lander's sensors also recorded the vibrations of wind.
story.nowStatus: The lander is retired at its landing site, centered at about 4.5° N, 135.9° E.

story.whatItIs: Ingenuity was a small helicopter that flew at Jezero Crater, Mars. It made its first flight on 19 April 2021 and flew 72 times.
story.whyLeft: Ingenuity flew for the last time on 18 January 2024, and its mission was completed on 25 January 2024. NASA's mission page gives no cause; the challenge description says rotor damage left it a stationary artifact.
story.science: NASA describes its first flight, on 19 April 2021, as the first powered flight on another planet, and it flew 72 times in total.
story.nowStatus: It remains at Jezero Crater. NASA's mission page does not give coordinates or describe its present condition.

sources.title: NASA GISS Mars24: Mars lander coordinates (map position only; Ingenuity uses the Jezero Crater landing site of Perseverance)

name: Phoenix lander

site.name: Phoenix site: Green Valley, Vastitas Borealis

modelCredit: Simplified stand-in built for this game; NASA 3D Resources has no downloadable Phoenix model in the set we used.

story.whatItIs: Phoenix was a NASA lander whose objective was to search for evidence of past or present microbial life. It launched on 4 August 2007 from Cape Canaveral, Florida, and landed on 25 May 2008 in the Green Valley of Vastitas Borealis, an arctic plain on Mars, at 68.22° N, 234.25° E.
story.whyLeft: The mission ended on 2 November 2008. NASA's mission page does not state the cause.
story.science: Phoenix verified water ice in the Martian subsurface: on 31 July 2008 NASA announced there is water on Mars, based on a sample analysed by the lander's TEGA instrument. It also found perchlorate in the soil, announced on 5 August 2008, a finding NASA described as neither confirming nor refuting the possibility of life.
story.nowStatus: Phoenix is no longer operating. It remains at its landing site in Vastitas Borealis.

name: Dawn spacecraft

site.name: In orbit around Ceres, main asteroid belt

modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Dawn (shown larger than life so you can see it)
whereabouts: In orbit around the dwarf planet Ceres in the main asteroid belt. NASA says it will remain there for decades: at least 20 years, with more than 99 percent confidence of at least 50 years.

story.whatItIs: NASA's Dawn was an orbiter that made extended stays at two small worlds in the main asteroid belt: the giant asteroid Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres. It launched on 27 September 2007. In 2011 it became the first spacecraft to orbit a body in the region between Mars and Jupiter, and in 2015 it became the first to visit a dwarf planet.
story.whyLeft: Dawn ran out of hydrazine, the fuel that lets it control its pointing. Without it, it can no longer aim its antennas at Earth or its solar panels at the Sun. It missed scheduled contacts on 31 October and 1 November 2018, and NASA's release of 1 November 2018 announced the end of the mission. NASA left it in orbit instead of sending it down: because Ceres has conditions of interest to scientists who study the chemistry that leads to life, NASA follows strict planetary protection protocols for disposing of the spacecraft.
story.science: Dawn let scientists compare two planet-like worlds that evolved very differently, and showed that location mattered to how objects formed and evolved in the early Solar System. NASA says its results reinforced the idea that dwarf planets could have hosted oceans over a significant part of their history.
story.nowStatus: Dawn is in orbit around Ceres, where NASA says it will remain for decades. NASA's pages do not give the shape of that orbit, so the circle drawn in the game is only illustrative.

sources.title: NASA: Dawn Mission to Asteroid Belt Comes to End (1 Nov 2018)
JPL Small-Body Database: Ceres (orbit drawn in the game, rounded)

name: NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft

site.name: On asteroid Eros, just south of the saddle-shaped feature Himeros

modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, NEAR Shoemaker (shown larger than life so you can see it)
whereabouts: On the surface of the asteroid 433 Eros, where it touched down on 12 February 2001 at 19:44 UT, just south of a saddle-shaped feature named Himeros. NASA's page gives only this touchdown area, not exact coordinates.

story.whatItIs: NASA calls NEAR the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid, and it was also the first to land on one. It launched on 17 February 1996 from Cape Canaveral, Florida, and was renamed NEAR Shoemaker in March 2000 to honour the geologist Eugene M. Shoemaker (1928–1997). Its target was the asteroid Eros.
story.whyLeft: NASA's page says the spacecraft was not designed as a lander, yet it survived a slow, controlled descent and touched down at about 4 mph (6.4 km/h) on 12 February 2001. Its last contact was on 28 February 2001, when the spacecraft succumbed to extreme cold (about minus 173 °C). A contact attempt on 10 December 2002 was unsuccessful. The page does not say why the landing was attempted.
story.science: NEAR found that Eros has no magnetic field. Its near-infrared spectrometer mapped more than 70 percent of the surface, and it returned about 10 times more data than planned, including 160,000 images. Eros turned out smaller than expected, with two medium-sized craters, a long surface ridge, and a density similar to Earth's crust.
story.nowStatus: NEAR Shoemaker is on Eros, near its touchdown area south of Himeros. NASA's page does not give its exact position on the asteroid; in the game it is placed on the asteroid's underside.

sources.title: NASA Science: NEAR Shoemaker mission page
JPL Small-Body Database: 433 Eros (orbit drawn in the game, rounded)

name: Pioneer 10 spacecraft

site.name: Heading toward the star Aldebaran, in Taurus, in interstellar space

modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Pioneer 10 (shown larger than life so you can see it)
whereabouts: Heading generally toward the red star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus, which NASA says it is expected to pass in about two million years. NASA's latest figure on its page is about 118.8 AU from Earth on 5 November 2017 (roughly 17.7 billion km); the game places it at that distance and does not extrapolate to today.

story.whatItIs: Pioneer 10 was NASA's first mission to the outer planets, launched on 2 March 1972 from Cape Canaveral, Florida. It was the first spacecraft to fly beyond Mars, cross the main asteroid belt, pass Jupiter, and cross Neptune's orbit (13 June 1983), the first on a trajectory to leave the Solar System, and the first to use all-nuclear electrical power. It was designed for a 21-month mission.
story.whyLeft: Routine contact ended on 31 March 1997 due to budgetary reasons. Later, its nuclear power source decayed until there was not enough power for the radio transmitter. The last signal was received on 23 January 2003 from about 12.23 billion km away; the signal took 11 hours 20 minutes to arrive. A final contact attempt on 4 March 2006 failed.
story.science: Scientists identified plasma in Jupiter's magnetic field. Pioneer 10 took about 500 images of Jupiter's atmosphere, including the Great Red Spot, and the first close-up images of Ganymede. Its data showed Jupiter's magnetic tail extends almost 800 million km, reaching Saturn's orbit. It also measured zodiacal light and met fewer asteroid hits than expected.
story.nowStatus: Still travelling outward toward Aldebaran. NASA's page does not give its current speed or position, so the game shows it at the 2017 distance NASA lists.

name: Pioneer 11 spacecraft

site.name: Heading out of the Solar System, toward the star Lambda Aquilae

modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Pioneer 10; used here for its sister craft, Pioneer 11 (shown larger than life so you can see it)
whereabouts: Heading out of the Solar System toward the centre of the galaxy, in the general direction of Sagittarius. NASA says it will pass near the star Lambda Aquilae in almost four million years. NASA's latest figure is about 97.59 AU from Earth on 5 November 2017 (14.599 billion km); the game places it at that distance, toward that star, and does not extrapolate to today.

story.whatItIs: Pioneer 11 was the sister craft to Pioneer 10, launched on 6 April 1973 from Cape Canaveral, Florida. It flew past Jupiter on 3 December 1974, about 42,500 km above the cloud tops, and on 1 September 1979 it became the first spacecraft to study Saturn up close and the first human-made object to fly past it.
story.whyLeft: NASA's page says the mission ended in 1995. NASA Ames made last contact on 30 September 1995, when the spacecraft was 44.1 AU from Earth. A few minutes of good engineering data were received on 24 November 1995, and contact was lost again once Earth moved out of view of the spacecraft's antenna.
story.science: At Jupiter it took the first pictures of the planet's polar regions and about 200 images of its moons. At Saturn it took 440 images, found a new ring (the F ring) and a new moon about 200 km across, and gave the first conclusive evidence of Saturn's magnetic field. Its data suggested Saturn is primarily liquid hydrogen.
story.nowStatus: Still travelling outward. NASA's page does not give its current position, so the game shows it at the 2017 distance NASA lists, in the direction of Lambda Aquilae.

name: Kepler space telescope

site.name: In orbit around the Sun, away from Earth

modelCredit: NASA 3D Resources, Kepler (A) (shown larger than life so you can see it)
whereabouts: In a heliocentric (Sun-centred) orbit. NASA retired it "within its current, safe orbit, away from Earth". NASA's pages give no distance from Earth, and the game's placement (a 371-day Earth-trailing orbit, the design figure from NASA's pre-launch planning) is approximate.

story.whatItIs: Kepler was NASA's first planet-hunting mission, a space telescope that searched for Earth-sized planets outside our Solar System. It launched on 6 March 2009 and became the agency's first mission to detect Earth-size planets in the habitable zones of their stars.
story.whyLeft: In May 2013 the loss of a second reaction wheel effectively ended new data collection for the original mission, and the extended K2 mission followed. Kepler then ran out of the fuel needed for further science operations. NASA announced on 30 October 2018 that the spacecraft was retired within its current, safe orbit, away from Earth.
story.science: Kepler leaves a legacy of more than 2,600 planet discoveries from outside our Solar System. The most common planet size it found is between Earth and Neptune, a size that does not exist in our own Solar System.
story.nowStatus: Kepler is in its retirement orbit around the Sun, away from Earth. NASA's pages do not state its exact position or distance.

sources.title: NASA: NASA Retires Kepler Space Telescope, Passes Planet-Hunting Torch (30 Oct 2018)
